name: Devghat
tagline: Where the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli become the Narayani
meta_description: Devghat, near Narayangadh: the sacred confluence of the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli, ashrams, the suspension bridge, the Maghe Sankranti mela and how to visit.
summary: Devghat is a Hindu pilgrimage site at the meeting of the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli rivers, about 7 km from Narayangadh. Pilgrims bathe at the confluence, elderly devotees retire here to live out their last years, and a huge mela is held at Maghe Sankranti in mid-January. Visit for a half day, any month.
intro: Seven kilometres north-west of Narayangadh, two of Nepal's great rivers meet. The Kali Gandaki, grey with glacial silt from Mustang, joins the greener Trishuli from the Rasuwa side, and from here on the river is called the Narayani. The meeting point is Devghat, the landing of the gods, one of the holiest bathing places in Nepal. Pilgrims have bathed here for generations, and the town has grown up around that daily act of devotion.

A long suspension bridge crosses the Trishuli between Chitwan and Tanahun districts, and on both banks temples, ashrams and simple houses climb the slope among trees. Many residents are elderly men and women who have come from all over Nepal and India to spend their last years beside the sacred water, reading scripture and bathing each morning. Mornings are calm, with bells, chanting and the sound of water; afternoons are slow and hot.

Devghat is an easy, rewarding half day from Sauraha or a stop on the road between Chitwan and Pokhara or Kathmandu. Come early to see pilgrims bathing in the cool light, cross the bridge, visit a temple or two, and sit by the river. In mid-January, at Maghe Sankranti, the quiet town fills with hundreds of thousands of pilgrims for one of Nepal's biggest melas. Outside the mela, it is one of the quietest places near Chitwan.

story.title: A riverside town for the last years of life
paras: Hindus have long treated river confluences as especially sacred, and Devghat, where the Kali Gandaki meets the Trishuli, is among the most important in Nepal. The Kali Gandaki carries saligram stones, black ammonite fossils from Mustang worshipped as forms of Vishnu, and bathing where it joins another river is believed to cleanse sins. Funeral rites are also performed here, because many Hindus believe that dying or being cremated at a sacred confluence helps the soul toward liberation.

For generations, devout Hindus have come here to spend their final years. Some build small huts; others live in ashrams run by religious trusts. The town has a Sanskrit college, ayurvedic services, health camps and projects for elderly residents, and the government has set up a development committee to manage the area and build sites for end-of-life rites. The result is a town where many residents are old, unhurried and devout, and where the day is measured by prayer times rather than shop hours.

The quiet daily rhythm, of bathing, prayer, study and simple meals, changes once a year. At Maghe Sankranti in mid-January, pilgrims arrive by bus, car and on foot from across Nepal and India to bathe at the confluence on the most auspicious day of the winter, and the riverbanks fill with stalls, sadhus and families. For one day Devghat becomes one of the busiest places in the country, and by evening the town returns to its quiet routine.

legend: Local tradition says the gods themselves came down to bathe at this meeting of rivers, which is why it is called Devghat, the gods' landing. Pilgrims also visit a cave that devotees associate with Sita, the heroine of the Ramayana. Bathing at the confluence on Maghe Sankranti is believed to bring great merit.
people: Devghat's residents are a mix of local Brahmin, Chhetri and Magar families, ashram staff, priests and Sanskrit students, and elderly pilgrims from across Nepal and India who have settled here for their final years. Bote families have long run ferries on these rivers. Nepali is the common language, with Hindi and Maithili heard among pilgrims.

untold.fact: Devghat sits where the Trishuli and Kali Gandaki meet, and below this confluence the river is called the Narayani, which forms the western edge of Chitwan National Park.
Maghe Sankranti draws huge crowds to Devghat each mid-January, making its mela one of the largest religious gatherings in Nepal; no one knows exactly when the tradition began.
A historic suspension bridge links the Tanahun and Chitwan sides of Devghat, and the town has a post-graduate Sanskrit college, the Mahesh Sanskrit Gurukul.

taste.name: Chaku and til laddu
taste.text: At Maghe Sankranti, families eat chaku, a hard sweet of molasses and ghee, til laddu made from sesame and jaggery, boiled sweet potato and tarul yam. Stalls at Devghat and sweet shops in Narayangadh sell them in January; tarul and sweet potato appear in markets through winter.

facts: Oct – Mar; mid-January for the mela
River confluence, ashrams, Maghe Sankranti mela

highlights.title: Dawn at the confluence
highlights.text: Arrive soon after sunrise to see pilgrims bathing where the grey Kali Gandaki meets the green Trishuli, offering water to the sun and lighting small lamps. The light and quiet make it Devghat's best hour.

highlights.title: The suspension bridge
highlights.text: A long footbridge crosses the Trishuli between Chitwan and Tanahun. Walk across for views down to the confluence and of the temples and ashrams on both banks. Hold the cables and walk at an even pace.

highlights.title: Ashrams and temples
highlights.text: Small temples, ashrams and shrines line the slopes. Visitors are welcome to look in quietly, and elderly residents are often happy to talk about why they came to live here. Remove shoes where asked.

highlights.title: Maghe Sankranti mela
highlights.text: In mid-January Devghat hosts one of Nepal's largest religious fairs. Pilgrims bathe at dawn, sadhus gather, and stalls sell sweets, sweet potatoes and religious items. Arrive before dawn and expect heavy traffic.

highlights.title: Saligram stones
highlights.text: The Kali Gandaki carries saligram fossils from Mustang. You may see them on altars and at stalls; they are sacred to Hindus and should not be taken from the river. Leave any you find where they lie.

how_to_reach.text: Devghat is about 7 km from Narayangadh, 15 to 20 minutes by car or local bus, and about 20 km from Sauraha, around 45 minutes. From Kathmandu or Pokhara, turn off near Narayangadh; it makes an easy stop on the way to or from Chitwan.
Within Devghat, walk the riverside paths and cross the suspension bridge on foot. Paths are uneven and steep in places, so wear comfortable shoes with grip.

where_to_stay: Most visitors come for a half day and stay in Sauraha, about 45 minutes away, or in Bharatpur, which has business hotels close to the airport. Devghat has simple ashram guesthouses used mainly by pilgrims; they are basic and follow religious routines. During the Maghe Sankranti mela, rooms in Narayangadh and Bharatpur fill quickly, so book early if you plan to attend.
tips: Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees, and remove shoes where asked.
Ask before photographing people bathing or praying, and never photograph cremations.
Do not swim; the currents at the confluence are strong even in the dry season.
For the Maghe Sankranti mela, arrive before dawn and expect large crowds and traffic.
Combine Devghat with Bishazari Tal or a taas lunch in Narayangadh for a full day.

experiences.title: Dawn with pilgrims at the confluence
experiences.summary: Arrive at first light to watch pilgrims bathe at the meeting of the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli, offer water to the rising sun and light butter lamps, as the two rivers of different colours become the Narayani.
body: Leave Sauraha before dawn for the 45-minute drive. As the light grows, residents and pilgrims make their way down stone steps to the water's edge. Men wade in to their waists, women bathe in saris, and many pour water from small copper pots toward the sun while reciting prayers. Some bathers bring small offerings of flowers and rice, which they release onto the current.

Look across the confluence and you can often see the two rivers running side by side before they mix: the Kali Gandaki grey with silt from the high Himalaya, the Trishuli clearer and greener. Priests sit on the steps with small offerings, and the smell of incense and marigolds drifts across the water. In winter, mist often hangs over the water until the sun is well up.

Stay quietly at the edge, ask before taking photographs and do not enter the water yourself unless invited and with care; the current is strong. Afterwards, walk up through the lanes to a tea stall and watch the town wake up. Most visitors spend an hour at the river, then return to Sauraha for a late breakfast or continue to Bishazari Tal.

faqs.q: Can tourists bathe at Devghat?
faqs.a: Visitors may join the ritual bath, but the current at the confluence is strong and the water cold in winter. Stay close to the steps in shallow water, never swim out, and follow local advice. Many visitors simply watch respectfully from the bank, which is perfectly acceptable.

faqs.q: Which rivers meet at Devghat?
faqs.a: The Kali Gandaki, which flows from Mustang through the deep gorge between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, and the Trishuli, which rises in Tibet and enters Nepal near Rasuwa, west of Langtang. Below Devghat the combined river is called the Narayani. Both rivers are fed by Himalayan snow and glaciers.

faqs.q: What time should I arrive at Devghat for sunrise?
faqs.a: Aim to arrive about 20 to 30 minutes before sunrise, roughly 6 am in winter and 5:30 am in spring. Leave Sauraha around 5 am. Fog in December and January can hide the rivers for the first hour, but the scene is still atmospheric.

experiences.title: Suspension bridge and ashram walk
experiences.summary: Cross the long suspension bridge between Chitwan and Tanahun, then wander the lanes of temples, ashrams and small houses on both banks, meeting elderly residents who have come to spend their final years by the river.
body: The suspension bridge over the Trishuli is Devghat's main street. From the middle you look down on the confluence, with boats and bathers below and forested hills rising behind. Pilgrims, schoolchildren, monks and porters cross constantly, and the bridge sways gently underfoot. Stop near the middle for the best view of where the two rivers meet.

On the far bank, lanes wind uphill past small temples to Shiva, Vishnu and the goddess, ashrams with courtyards and libraries, and simple houses where elderly residents live. Many came from distant parts of Nepal or India to live near the sacred water. Some are glad to talk, in Nepali or Hindi, about why they chose Devghat. Many speak with pride of the place and its quiet.

Your guide can point out the Sanskrit college, ayurvedic centres and the sites set aside for final rites. Walk slowly, greet people with namaste, and keep your voice low inside temple grounds. The walk is steep in places but short. Allow two to three hours and carry water; there are tea stalls but few shops. Afternoons are hot from March onward.

faqs.q: Is the Devghat suspension bridge safe?
faqs.a: Yes, it is used every day by residents and pilgrims. It sways a little as people walk, which some visitors find unsettling. Hold the side cables, walk at an even pace, and avoid stopping in large groups in the middle. People with a strong fear of heights may prefer to watch from the bank.

faqs.q: Why do elderly people live in Devghat?
faqs.a: For many Hindus, living and dying beside a sacred river confluence brings religious merit. Elderly devotees come to Devghat to spend their final years in prayer, study and ritual bathing, living in ashrams or small houses. Some are supported by family, others by religious trusts.

faqs.q: Can I visit the ashrams in Devghat?
faqs.a: Many ashrams welcome respectful visitors to their courtyards and temples during the day. Remove shoes where asked, dress modestly and do not interrupt prayers. A small donation is appreciated but not required. Ask your guide which ashrams are open to visitors.

experiences.title: Maghe Sankranti mela at Devghat
experiences.summary: On the first day of Magh, usually 14 or 15 January, Devghat hosts one of Nepal's largest melas. Pilgrims bathe at dawn, sadhus gather, and stalls sell chaku, til laddu and sweet potatoes along the riverbank.
body: Maghe Sankranti marks the sun's move into Capricorn and the end of the coldest, least auspicious month. Across Nepal people bathe in rivers and eat warming foods, but the confluence at Devghat is one of the most important places to do it. Pilgrims arrive overnight and wait on the banks for first light. Many pilgrims sleep near the riverbank, wrapped in blankets beside small fires.

At dawn the crowds go down to the water in waves. Families bathe together, priests chant, and offerings of flowers, rice and coins float away. Sadhus sit by fires along the bank. Stalls sell chaku, til laddu, sweet potatoes, tarul, religious pictures and toys, and loudspeakers announce lost children. Families eat chaku, til laddu and sweet potato on the bank after bathing.

It is crowded, noisy and moving. Go with a guide, keep valuables secure, and agree on a meeting point. Roads near Narayangadh become very slow, so leave Sauraha early and expect a long return. Wear warm clothes and comfortable shoes, carry water and snacks, and keep phones and cash in an inside pocket. Ask before taking close portraits of bathers or sadhus.

faqs.q: When is Maghe Sankranti at Devghat?
faqs.a: Maghe Sankranti falls on the first day of the month of Magh in the Nepali calendar, usually 14 or 15 January. The main bathing is at dawn that day, though crowds build the evening before. Check current status before you travel for the exact date each year.

faqs.q: How crowded is the Devghat mela?
faqs.a: Very. Hundreds of thousands of pilgrims are reported in big years, and roads to Devghat jam from before dawn. Expect pushing near the steps, long walks from parking and noise all day. It is a powerful experience but not for anyone who dislikes crowds.

faqs.q: Is Maghe Sankranti the same as Maghi?
faqs.a: They fall on the same day. Hindus across Nepal call it Maghe Sankranti and mark it with river baths and warming foods. Tharu communities celebrate the same day as Maghi, their new year, with family feasts, dhikri and dancing. In Chitwan you can see both.

experiences.title: Chaku, til and tarul: winter festival foods
experiences.image_query: chaku til laddu Maghe Sankranti food
experiences.summary: Taste the foods of Maghe Sankranti at Devghat and in Narayangadh: chaku molasses sweet, sesame til laddu, boiled sweet potato and tarul yam, eaten in mid-January to warm the body at the turn of winter.
body: Food is central to Maghe Sankranti. Families believe the cold of Poush must be balanced with warming, rich foods, so they eat ghee, molasses, sesame and root vegetables. At Devghat during the mela, stalls pile up chaku, a hard brown sweet made by boiling sugarcane molasses with ghee. Each family has its own preferences, and the foods differ between hill and plains communities.

Til laddu are balls of roasted sesame bound with jaggery, sold in paper bags. Sweet potato and tarul, a large yam, are boiled and eaten with salt or a little ghee. Some families add spinach and ghee rice, and in Tharu homes nearby the day brings dhikri and meat curries for Maghi. Tarul is boiled until soft and has a starchy, slightly sweet taste.

Outside the festival, sweet shops in Narayangadh sell til laddu and chaku through the winter. Your guide can help you buy some to take home, though chaku can be very hard; break off small pieces and let them soften in your mouth. Til laddu travel well in luggage; chaku can soften in heat, so keep it cool.

faqs.q: What is chaku?
faqs.a: Chaku is a hard, dark sweet made by boiling sugarcane molasses, sometimes with ghee and nuts, until it sets. It is eaten in Nepal at Maghe Sankranti in mid-January and is believed to warm the body. You can buy it at stalls and sweet shops during the festival.

faqs.q: Why do Nepalis eat sweet potatoes at Maghe Sankranti?
faqs.a: Root vegetables such as sweet potato and tarul yam are harvested in winter and considered warming foods. Eating them with ghee and sesame at Maghe Sankranti is a tradition across Nepal, marking the move from the coldest month toward longer, warmer days.

faqs.q: Can I buy Sankranti sweets outside January?
faqs.a: Some sweet shops in Narayangadh and Kathmandu sell til laddu and chaku through the winter months, but the widest choice is in the weeks around Maghe Sankranti in mid-January. Outside winter they are harder to find. Ask your guide to point out a good shop.

faqs.q: Where is Devghat?
faqs.a: Devghat is at the confluence of the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli rivers, about 7 km north-west of Narayangadh, on the border of Chitwan and Tanahun districts. It is about 20 km from Sauraha, around 45 minutes by road, and easy to reach from the Kathmandu–Narayangadh and Pokhara–Narayangadh roads.

faqs.q: Why is Devghat sacred?
faqs.a: Hindus consider river confluences especially holy, and Devghat joins two major rivers, the Kali Gandaki and the Trishuli, which become the Narayani. Bathing here is believed to cleanse sins, and many elderly devotees choose to spend their final years by the confluence. The name means the landing place of the gods.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Devghat?
faqs.a: Two to three hours is enough for most visitors: the confluence, a walk over the suspension bridge and a visit to a temple or ashram. Come at sunrise for the bathing. Combine it with Bishazari Tal or lunch in Narayangadh to make a half or full day from Sauraha.

faqs.q: Is Devghat worth visiting from Chitwan?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are interested in Hindu culture, rivers and quiet places. It shows a side of the Terai that safaris do not, and it is close to Sauraha. It also makes a good stop on the drive between Chitwan and Pokhara or Kathmandu.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Devghat?
faqs.a: October to March for comfortable weather, with mid-January for the Maghe Sankranti mela. Early morning is the best time of day. From June to September the rivers run high and fast; the bridge and temples stay open, but riverbank access is limited.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus enter temples at Devghat?
faqs.a: Most temples and ashrams at Devghat welcome respectful visitors of any faith to their courtyards, but some inner shrines are for Hindus only. Watch for signs, ask your guide, remove shoes where required and dress modestly. When in doubt, stay in the courtyard.

faqs.q: Are there cremations at Devghat?
faqs.a: Yes, Devghat is used for Hindu funeral rites, and you may see cremations at the riverbank. Treat them with respect: keep your distance, do not take photographs and stay quiet. Ask your guide where to stand if a ceremony is in progress.

faqs.q: What is the Maghe Sankranti mela at Devghat?
faqs.a: It is a large religious fair held on the first day of Magh, usually 14 or 15 January, when hundreds of thousands of pilgrims bathe at the confluence. Sadhus, stalls and families fill the banks. Check current status before you travel for the date and traffic arrangements.

faqs.q: Can I see saligram stones at Devghat?
faqs.a: Yes. Saligrams, black ammonite fossils carried by the Kali Gandaki from Mustang, are worshipped as forms of Vishnu and seen on altars and sometimes at stalls. They are sacred, and exporting fossils from Nepal may be restricted, so check the rules before buying one.
